#5485. Opinion: How Kennedy and MAHA could help stop measles

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”

On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”

Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …

It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.

Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.

Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.

I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?

I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.

Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.

I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.

They’ve also given me a front-row seat to something else: the MAHA grassroots movement’s astonishing ability to organize.

I’ve watched as MAHA supporters rally around pesticides, toxic pollutants in our air and water, microplastics, and PFAS (aka “forever”) chemicals. I’ve been to conferences and meetings, and been included in many group chats and Zoom meetings, where you can practically feel the energy around you: people exchanging ideas, meeting with lawmakers to draft legislation, and mobilizing others to organize local action. I constantly hear two questions: “What do you need? How can I help?”

That energy doesn’t seem to have disappeared after the midterms. But it’s definitely looking for places to go.

MAHA is politically weak right now. Candidates backed by the movement suffered significant electoral defeats, and there’s anger at the Trump administration over what seem like broken promises on pesticides, corporate influence, and environmental health. Yet the grassroots supporters haven’t given up. They’ve already been regrouping around issues like data centers and their effects on communities, while continuing to fight toxic pollutants and corporate influence. They don’t want to wait for the government or medical establishment to fix problems for them.

Measles presents a different kind of challenge. Public health officials need to reach parents who hesitate before vaccinating their children, including families in communities that view government institutions with suspicion.

I’ve heard from public health officials that many local health departments are so underfunded, they struggle to reach these families — and even when they have the resources, they may lack the cultural fluency or trusted relationships to connect with them.

But what if some of the people who could help actually share those families’ skepticism about pharmaceutical companies, admire Kennedy, or prefer alternative medicine — yet believe the MMR vaccine is worth getting?

MAHA is not a fringe movement. According to KFF’s analysis of the 2026 midterm election, roughly 3 in 10 voters said they support MAHA, including 21% who strongly support it.

And, perhaps surprisingly, most MAHA-supporting parents vaccinate their kids. A separate KFF/Washington Post survey found that 86% of MAHA-supporting parents believe it’s important for children in their communities to be vaccinated against measles. Nearly 8 in 10 expressed confidence in the safety of the MMR vaccine. And about 75% reported that their children were up to date on routine childhood vaccinations, excluding Covid and flu.

Truthfully, very few MAHA supporters I’ve met haven’t taken MMR or vaccinated their children against polio, even if on a delayed schedule. I’ve met plenty who feel differently about Covid, flu, or the hep B birth dose, and certainly there are those who reject MMR. But among rank-and-file supporters, I’ve encountered far fewer MMR skeptics than you might expect from listening to some of the movement’s most prominent influencers. Which is important for the challenge at hand: You can believe deeply in MAHA’s core concerns about food, pesticides, water, chronic disease, and even have mistrust in flu and Covid shots — but still have confidence in the value of the measles vaccine.

We don’t acknowledge this enough. Some of MAHA’s most prominent vaccine skeptics may not speak for the broader movement when it comes to MMR.

The science on MMR is clear: Two doses are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles. But knowing the facts and trusting the person delivering them are two very different things. A fact like that can land differently when it comes from someone who has wrestled with the same doubts you have.

I think about Roberta Devers, a mother and midwife practicing in Lancaster County, Pa., whom my colleagues and I met working on an episode about the measles outbreak there.

Roberta was vaccine skeptical, a Kennedy supporter, and chose not to vaccinate her son when he was a baby. But after seeing what measles was doing to people in Lancaster County, she changed her mind. She believes MMR is effective against measles and encourages Amish families in outbreak areas to get vaccinated, too. She tells me she now gets one or two calls a week from families who want to get vaccinated.

What’s particularly interesting to me, though, is what hasn’t changed.

Roberta still admires Kennedy. She hasn’t suddenly decided the medical establishment deserves her trust. If anything, she tells me the measles outbreaks are a reflection of a lack of trust communities continue to have for health systems. One of her ongoing campaigns is to fight for home-birth midwives to receive the same recognition as those working in hospitals. She talks about holistic living, alternative medicine, eating whole foods, even using brown paper toilet paper because she believes in living close to the earth. She hasn’t changed her values or worldview. She’s simply reconsidered what she believes about measles vaccination.

Imagine a vaccine-hesitant parent hearing from someone like Roberta, who shares many of their concerns but has seen measles up close and reached a different conclusion. Roberta doesn’t need to defend pharmaceutical companies or persuade anyone that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is always right. Just telling her story could lead to a conversation that perhaps a public health official would have a harder time brokering.

I’m not suggesting this movement will suddenly lead the charge on getting Americans vaccinated for measles. Some of MAHA’s most influential voices have spent years not just questioning, but actively sowing distrust in vaccines, including MMR, using claims not rooted in scientific fact. And I expect for many, encouraging vaccination, even during an outbreak, would be a bridge too far for them, a betrayal of their principles.

And organizing a rally isn’t the same as running a public health response.

But shouldn’t we at least try to make an active effort to reach MAHA supporters who believe in MMR? Because the polling shows it looks like there are a lot of them.

In his statement, Kennedy said his department is working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. He also promised to collaborate with trusted health care providers and community leaders.

He could start by elevating voices who support MMR. People like Devers, who can speak to vaccine-hesitant families with credibility and trust that public health institutions often lack. Find more people like her.

Then encourage those MAHA supporters who trust the measles vaccine to organize conversations about measles prevention. Bring in trusted physicians or other clinicians to answer questions. But also listen to families’ fears and doubts — because chances are, many MAHA supporters have wrestled with those same questions themselves. Help families find vaccines. Connect them with parents who share their values but have decided to vaccinate their children.

Would everyone in MAHA welcome that effort? Almost certainly not. Would Kennedy face backlash from the anti-vaccine wing of his movement? Very likely.

But for the past two years, MAHA supporters have pushed back against being characterized as anti-vaccine. Instead, they say, they are concerned about mandates, informed consent, conflicts of interest, and what they see as an unwillingness to acknowledge questions about safety.

Well, guys, here’s an opportunity to demonstrate what that distinction means in practice.

If you’re not anti-vaccine, helping people make informed decisions about a vaccine that the overwhelming majority of your own supporters trust shouldn’t betray your principles. It should express them.

The public health establishment has a responsibility here, too. If people within MAHA are willing to help, officials should work with them. That doesn’t mean overlooking misinformation or compromising on evidence. But it does mean recognizing common ground.

I know some readers will think I’m naive. Doesn’t she get that parts of MAHA have contributed to the distrust that makes measles prevention so difficult? I do. But even if parts of MAHA contributed to the problem, isn’t it worth asking whether some of its supporters might be particularly well positioned to contribute to the solution?

At a moment when MAHA is regrouping after an election rout, the movement now has an opportunity to demonstrate that it truly offers a big tent. Not by abandoning its core priorities, but by directing some of its powerful grassroots energy toward a disease affecting American children and their parents — the very people MAHA claims to put at the center of its mission.

Brinda Adhikari is a journalist and co-host of the “Why Should I Trust You?” podcast.

#5484. CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for new entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give plans greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

In addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low."

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health."

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy said in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs."

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

#5483. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening

Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

#5482. Opinion: When should medical school start?

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Torie Bosch is the First Opinion editor at STAT.

First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.

To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.

The authors’ proposal hinges on the premise that learning the foundational sciences and learning to become a physician can be separated without compromising either. My first year of medical school was peppered with clinical exposure and taught me otherwise. I floundered with a blood pressure cuff during a wellness visit, fumbled for words as I interviewed a man waiting for a heart transplant, and listened to a patient recount her immense sorrow after multiple miscarriages. These encounters remain among my most formative.

I agree with the authors that students are often preoccupied with medical licensure exams, and that early clinical exposure might not cure this. In my experience, however, it is the strongest counterweight. After meeting those patients, I was learning for more than an exam. The proposed model would abandon that counterweight. Students would still encounter patients eventually, but we would have forfeited valuable time. Becoming a compassionate, humanistic physician is slow work, and it deserves all the time we can offer. A flashcard can teach a student what causes a miscarriage. It takes a patient to teach what it means to grieve one. And that lesson should not wait until after Step 1.

— Surya Pulukuri, Harvard Medical School student

Markovich is correct: The U.S. health care “non-system” is broken. There are many culprits, including hospitals, whose prices are set more by market dominance than by quality. He should also look at the administrative complexity driven largely by our myriad of private insurance companies. Some 25% of U.S. “health care” spending goes to administrative costs. The insurers need to agree on a single set of billing codes and procedures to cut doctors’ and hospitals’ cost of billing. They need to sit down with doctors and come up with a uniform set of procedures needing pre-authorization and a single set of criteria. They need to agree on a small number of policy options that are understandable to the public. Finger-pointing is easy, but should start at home.

— Edward Hoffer, M.D., Harvard Medical School

A chatbot can handle every conversation responsibly and still, over time, take the place of someone a person used to confide in. In their First Opinion essay, Qian Yang, Ned Cooper, and Ibrahim Emara show how easily a gradual loss of human connection can escape safeguards designed for individual conversations. They make a persuasive case for giving independent researchers access to platform data and developing tools to distinguish the effects of chatbot use from other causes of isolation. Those tools should ask whether people could reach someone they trusted when they needed help.

That question is especially worth asking adolescents, who may have fewer ways to seek help privately. Imagine two teenagers who each spend an hour every night talking to a chatbot. One used to call a friend during difficult times, but he called less often as talking to the chatbot became a habit. The other still talks to friends every day. When she wanted to discuss something she feared would get back to her parents, she asked to see a school counselor. While she waited for an appointment, she took the problem to a chatbot. Their chat logs might look very similar. The authors suggest measuring school counselor time as one way to estimate what isolation costs schools. That measure captures time counselors spend helping students. Hours, days, or weeks spent waiting leave no trace.

Researchers could ask teens to think about the last time something was troubling them. Did they talk to someone about it, try to reach someone, or decide against reaching out? If they tried, did they get to talk to someone? Did they talk to a chatbot about it?

Asking these questions regularly could help researchers distinguish a teen who reached out to people less often as their chatbot usage grew from one who turned to a chatbot only after trying to get help. The distinction matters for policymaking. When chatbot use displaces human contact, usage limits may help. When it fills a gap in support, the priority should be making help easier to reach. A usage limit might prompt one teenager to call a friend. Another may still be waiting for someone to call back.

— Brian J. Carter, J.D., Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

In her essay “How bad is healthy supposed to feel?” Kirsten Balin properly notes that medicine has a regrettable history of dismissing symptoms, particularly in women. However, she also says that health professionals tend to give an illness label to the aches, pains, and anxieties of everyday living when the symptoms have no underlying biological explanation. As examples, she lists chronic fatigue syndrome and autonomic dysfunction. In fact, there are tens of thousands of peer-reviewed publications in top scientific journals that document the biological abnormalities in these two illnesses. The same is true with several other similar illnesses such as fibromyalgia and long Covid. It now is clear that they all are “real” illnesses.

— Anthony L. Komaroff, M.D., Harvard Medical School

The authors of the First Opinion commentary on pediatric emergencies from Oct. 27 identify a growing but hidden problem: stark gaps in delivery of pediatric emergency care across the U.S. The solutions they propose — payment reform, expanding regional care coordination hubs, and incentivizing large pediatric medical centers to support smaller hospitals — all merit serious consideration.

However, such approaches risk overlooking existing strengths that we can build upon now to support emergency departments and prehospital agencies aiming to develop their own internal capacity. Pediatric readiness refers to the infrastructure and resources EDs and prehospital agencies need to provide high-quality care for children. In our roles as researchers and physicians, we collaborate in community-engaged research to identify strategies to support EDs and EMS agencies in their readiness.

This is vital: EDs with high pediatric readiness have up to 76% lower mortality for critically ill children. It would cost approximately $200 million to make all EDs nationwide pediatric ready, a tiny fraction of annual U.S. health care expenditures. Many EDs lack designated pediatric champions, knowns as pediatric emergency care coordinators (PECCs), whose presence has been shown to be closely associated with readiness. As the authors rightly point out, larger pediatric medical centers can support smaller hospitals and PECCs.

That’s why we collaborate with local, national, and international partners in readiness improvement strategies such as telehealth support to smaller hospitals, simulation-based systems-testing and medical education, developing PECC networking and mentorship models, and more. This research stems from our experiences in rural, indigenous, and urban hospital systems. This has helped us understand the importance of foregrounding community members’ concerns and supporting their local expertise and leadership in our research efforts.

The authors grounded their commentary in two stories of what pediatricians are seeing nationwide. We agree that stories from families and local providers should drive our research. For us, that means collecting stories about what pediatric emergency readiness should look like, collaborating with community hospitals and families to identify research questions and select appropriate methodologies, and finding sustainable dissemination and implementation strategies.

EDs can start their own readiness journey by participating in the National Pediatric Readiness Project’s national assessment to identify current strengths and opportunities for improvement. As we work toward a future where any child can receive high-quality emergency care when and where they need it, we recommend starting by identifying and building upon strengths already in place.

— Elizabeth Sanseau, M.D., Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) PolicyLab, CHOP Indigenous Health Unit, and the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine; and Jeremy Jones, M.D., CHOP PolicyLab

As a pediatric emergency physician and clinical ethicist, I have experienced and witnessed aggression at work many times. The authors’ concern comes from a good place, but it misses the realities of the clinical setting. They write that ineffective signs would be “pointless, but not harmful.” I disagree, for three reasons.

First, the essay overstates the evidence against signage. Its claim rests on two sources: a 2006 survey of Australian nurses and a 2008 commentary on the U.K.’s zero tolerance campaign. Neither evaluates whether signs change behavior. Nor has anyone tested the claim that signs erode patient trust. Research on violence prevention is methodologically weak, though multicomponent programs show mixed but encouraging results.

Second, deterrence is not the only purpose of a sign. Even if the signs prevented nothing, they would matter. The authors acknowledge that violence against health care workers has risen. In emergency departments specifically, it has introduced a mental and physical burden that fundamentally changes what it means to do this work. Signage stating an obvious standard of behavior may seem trivial, but it can have meaning as a piece of a broader institutional commitment to health care worker well-being. It tells staff that their hospital understands the realities of their work and supports them.

Third, signs remind clinicians where their obligations end. Many clinicians, especially trainees, are unsure what they owe a patient or family who is abusing them. A hospital must screen and stabilize anyone who comes to the emergency department, whatever their behavior. Beyond that, no patient or family is entitled to further care from a clinician they are making unsafe. This is easy to forget amid the pressures of clinical care, and a visible reminder helps.

The authors worry about the message these signs send to patients and families. That concern is thoughtful, but it is aimed at the wrong signs. The signs I see in emergency departments name physical assault, threats, and harassment. A sign that polices tone or discourages complaints could deserve criticism, but those signs are the exception and should not set the terms of this debate. Even the authors want their alternative signs to make clear that violence will not be tolerated. They close by asking that the words on hospital walls communicate medicine’s values. Protecting the people who care for patients is one of them.

— Joseph Shapiro, M.D., Children’s National Hospital

Torie Bosch is the First Opinion editor at STAT.

#5481. Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians

Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure company, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

The option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

The patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is new is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

“AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”

In the new interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

From there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

#5480. As diabetes association’s turmoil continues, what does it mean for patients?

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Liz covers cardiovascular and metabolic disease, asking why we’re not doing better or even losing ground against the world’s leading killer. Send tips on Signal at LizC.22.

Five months after the American Diabetes Association fractured over a political protest and its extended fallout, one question remains unanswered.

What’s the bottom line for people living with diabetes?

Although any impact on patients may be hard to trace now, experts told STAT, they expressed concern that the impasse could stymie advancement in diabetes care. At the heart of the matter is the role the ADA and other professional organizations play in setting guidelines and sharing research, whether in their journals or at wide-ranging meetings that attract thousands to present and to learn.

The ADA dispute began after five members were ousted from its 2026 scientific meeting in New Orleans. The sparring continues, fueled by high-profile resignations and dismissals, a 1,221-member boycott, and the appointment of unidentified editors to manage journals. In October, an internal ADA review acknowledged some missteps but doubled down on its rebukes of members who objected to Trump administration policies decimating scientific research and proposing political reviews of individual projects.

A scheduled appearance by Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, inspired the five members to pass out copies of an editorial published in an ADA journal critical of diminished NIH funding. He did not appear, but armed security officers evicted those who shared the printouts outside the hall where he was expected to speak.

Bhattacharya was not the speaker originally suggested for the meeting, Mark Atkinson, who resigned as ADA’s 2026 scientific sessions planning committee chair, told STAT. His choice was to assemble a panel of academic experts to discuss artificial intelligence and its influence on diabetes care, but ADA leadership and its advocacy committee selected Bhattacharya instead.

These and other details regarding the dispute have accumulated, along with high-level resignations. But when asked if the continuing controversy matters to patients, the answer from four prominent voices is yes, but maybe not yet.

To illustrate his concern for the ADA’s future, Atkinson cited examples of how the ADA helped patients in the past.

“The ADA is one of many agencies that have advocated for lower insulin costs,” he told STAT. “They’re one of many agencies that have argued for increased federal funding for research. They’re advocates for standards of care.”

David Nathan, a noted researcher and founder of the Diabetes Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, is far more concerned about the broader impact of federal funding cuts on the scientific enterprise than he is about ADA tumult. Still, he’s also hearing from people who link that ongoing national crisis to what has happened at ADA.

They’re afraid of what’s going to happen to diabetes research, he said, starting with the NIH withdrawing support and then aggravated by the ADA discord.

“It’s really one blow on top of another,” Nathan told STAT. “All of this has coalesced to make everyone anxious, uncertain about the future of diabetes research. And the ADA should at this point be standing up and being something that we can all rally behind. Instead it is being fractured by its own actions.”

In a written response to STAT’s request for comment, the ADA press team said Tuesday, “The ADA has outlined the next steps that we plan to take to learn and improve based on the facts that came to bear from the review. This includes a review of event protocols, procedures, and code of conduct.”

In the near term, the 2027 ADA guidelines to be issued in December were already close to completion, physicians familiar with their production told STAT. The ADA confirmed their publication online in Diabetes Care next month. The agenda for the next annual scientific sessions, slated for June in Washington, D.C., is not yet set.

Meanwhile, the journals have been in limbo.

Since June, the ADA member boycott has erased the editorial masthead for Diabetes Care, its flagship journal. Editor-in-chief Steven Kahn, one of the five escorted out this past June, is part of the boycott, as are deputy editors. Chris Kohler, vice president of publications at ADA, resigned in protest when an interim editorial board was appointed without making their names public.

Kohler’s resignation letter said the appointment of unidentified interim editors violated editorial independence, scientific integrity, transparency, and accountability.

“I cannot, in good conscience, endorse or assume responsibility for an approach that I believe will compound the very problems it is intended to solve,” his Nov. 6 letter said.

Nathan, too, was severe about the unidentified editorial board. “To put it in strike terminology, these are scabs,” Nathan said. “I hate to tarnish them in that way, but they are working against this boycott. And the ADA has not announced the name of a single one of them. That’s weird.”

ADA told STAT the names would be made public.

“While the boycott continues, the ADA will remain relentless in our work to provide the resources that healthcare professionals are counting on. That is why we have established an interim editorial board for Diabetes Care that consists of highly experienced and respected healthcare professionals who have dedicated their careers to caring for people living with diabetes, including endocrinologists, primary care physicians focused on diabetes care, diabetes educators, and more,” the ADA press statement said. “The names of the interim editorial board will be placed on the Diabetes Care website soon.”

Elizabeth Selvin, a deputy editor at Diabetes Care who is also boycotting ADA, expressed concern that a weakened journals might dilute future guidelines.

“I worry that the CEO is treating the journal as a marketing tool for the organization rather than a scientific asset that should be protected and governed by standard publishing ethics,” she wrote to STAT about chief executive Charles Henderson. “A concern is that because typical governance structures to ensure editorial independence are not in place, we need to simply trust that ADA is not making decisions that will benefit industry more than patients.”

In its message to STAT, the ADA said the current editorial team’s term was set to end in December 2027. ADA has opened applications for a new editor-in-chief and said it will work with the selected candidate to confirm a transition plan and the appointment of deputy editors and associate editors.

In addition to the journals, large meetings are another forum for scientific exchange.

John Buse, an endocrinologist at the University of North Carolina and a former president of the ADA, is looking elsewhere.

“I am currently not submitting papers to any ADA journals, but there are many other outstanding journals to pick from,” he wrote to STAT. “It pains me, as of my 600 or so publications, no journal has published more of them than Diabetes Care historically.”

Journals are the way to communicate, Atkinson said.

“Without having medical journals, you don’t have a real way to impact how patients are treated in their care,” he said about the impasse. “This has just got to end soon because the losers in all of this are people with diabetes.”

The same holds true for scientific meetings. Buse plans to attend the Endocrine Society meeting in Toronto, which he has previously gone to only infrequently. He does regularly go to the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, which will meet this year in Budapest, calling it a strong meeting with much to offer. Another option is the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology meeting in San Diego.

“I do hope the issues are resolved soon and that I will attend the ADA, but the plan today is not to attend the scientific sessions in D.C. in June,” he wrote. “If the negotiations with ADA go nowhere and the boycott persists, there is great risk that the ADA loses its standing as the authoritative voice in diabetes. I am sure that the Endocrine Society, AACE, EASD, and others could carry the mantle in the future if the diaspora of thought leaders persists.”

Nathan said he and his colleagues are also thinking about where to present the results of their research, predicting scientists will find other venues. And so will participants and sponsors.

“Industry is interested in having a large audience at these annual meetings. If they start leaving, or if their support starts weakening, the ADA will suffer from it,” Nathan said. “As will people with diabetes. As will the scientific enterprise. I mean, this is just a colossal blunder on the part of the ADA.”

The ADA said there are plans to meet with some of the people leading the boycott to work towards a resolution.”

“They seem to be procrastinating, frankly, with us,” he said. “We have tried to get a meeting with them for easily more than four months. I think they’re hoping that this will just go away, and it’s not going away.”

STAT’s coverage of chronic health issues is supported by a grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

#5479. A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding

Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

Materials provided by Brigham and Women's Hospital. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
