#5415. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision.  At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

That said, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Coming back to the AI inference issue. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

In this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:

We see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

This means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

#5414. Rene Haas to Take Over Nvidia? What Will Happen to Crypto?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Nvidia could be about to hand its biggest job to the man who helped turn Arm into one of the world’s most valuable chip companies. Rene Haas is now being considered as a potential successor to Jensen Huang at Nvidia, a familiar face at the center of the AI industry’s biggest leadership change.

Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s recruitment firm had approached Haas as part of its search for a new chief executive. Haas previously spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since overseen its expansion into the booming AI infrastructure market.

Rene Haas has been approached regarding the CEO role at Nvidia by recruiting firm Heidrick & Struggles, which was hired by the board to replace Jensen Huang https://t.co/yiJ6NkvEtS

An appointment would put someone with experience at both companies in charge of Nvidia’s next chapter. But what does it mean for crypto? Could Haas push the AI boom even further, and what would that mean for Bitcoin and the rest of the market?

Haas is not an outsider to Nvidia. He previously ran the company’s computing products business between 2006 and 2013, giving him direct experience with the company before its transformation into an AI powerhouse.

His subsequent run at Arm offers a glimpse of what he might bring to the role. Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for its fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. Its profit before tax climbed from $756 million to $960 million. The company has also moved beyond its traditional chip-design licensing business, introducing its own AGI CPU for AI data centers in March 2026.

Arm’s technology already reaches more than 99% of smartphones sold worldwide. Its designs also power computing infrastructure used by major cloud providers and Nvidia itself.

Haas helped position the company for a much larger role in the AI economy. Now, his next challenge could be taking Nvidia beyond selling the chips powering that expansion.

Nvidia’s existing business gives him an enormous starting point. The company generated $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue in its latest results, with data center sales accounting for $107.6 billion. Revenue increased 103% from a year earlier.

Its next-generation Vera Rubin platform has also entered production and begun shipping. A new CEO would inherit an extraordinary growth engine, but also the responsibility of deciding how aggressively Nvidia should expand its influence across the AI industry.

If Haas brings his Arm strategy to Nvidia, we could see a push into integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure and new AI applications. That could create another wave of investment across the technology sector.

Crypto could benefit if Haas turns Nvidia’s next chapter into another catalyst for AI infrastructure spending. The connection extends beyond tokens carrying artificial intelligence branding. Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved in tandem with technology stocks during periods when investors shift between risk assets.

A stronger Nvidia could help restore confidence in the AI investment cycle, especially if investors believe its leadership transition will not interrupt infrastructure spending.

Decentralized computing projects such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash could also benefit. These networks are trying to capture demand for GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

More spending on AI infrastructure would create opportunities for decentralized alternatives. Developers need computing power, and centralized providers cannot always meet every requirement at the right price.

The bigger opportunity could come from investor appetite rather than immediate demand for crypto tokens. If Nvidia shares regain momentum under Rene Haas, technology investors could become more comfortable taking risks elsewhere. That would give crypto a potential source of buying interest.

Haas has already demonstrated what he can do with Arm. Taking over Nvidia would give him a considerably larger platform, with consequences extending well beyond semiconductor stocks.

#5413. Rare 25-Foot-Wide Carnegie Hill Townhouse With a Private Carriage House Lists for $11.95 Million

A 25-foot-wide townhouse with a carriage house has just hit the market for $11.95 million in Manhattan’s Carnegie Hill.

Built in 1899, the five-bedroom residence underwent a “no-expense-spared” reconstruction and features 13 newly renovated rooms, each with individually zoned heating and cooling.

“It is certainly very rare for a listing like this townhouse with a carriage house to come on the market in uptown Manhattan,” said listing agent Daniella G. Schlisser of Brown Harris Stevens. “I don’t recall ever seeing something like this here.”

The 7,700-square-foot interior was entirely gutted and rebuilt with new structural steel, plumbing, electrical, and commercial-grade mechanical systems.

“It has incredible sun and light, which is incredibly unusual for a townhouse,” Schlisser said. “The home is flooded with direct sunlight facing the back and it also gets sun to the north in the front.”

The six-story dwelling features a garden level that leads to a limestone gallery with custom paneling. There is a separately accessed commercial space offering “continued retail or office use” that could also be transformed into additional living space. French doors open to a bluestone-decked garden with a built-in grill.

“There is a phenomenal amount of space and light, and being a 25-foot-wide townhouse is also rare,” she noted.

A parlor level boasts a living room with a fireplace and herringbone floors. The nearby formal dining room was designed for grand-scale entertaining. Also on this level is a garden-facing eat-in kitchen with a breakfast bar, granite countertops, custom cabinetry, and high-end appliances.

The third floor has two en-suite bedrooms and a den with coffered ceilings, a wood-burning fireplace, and access to a private terrace overlooking the carriage house.

Two king-sized bedroom suites with custom "study" areas are on the fourth floor.

A lavish primary suite spans the entire fifth floor. It features a south-facing sitting room that opens to a private terrace, a windowed dressing room, and a spa-inspired bathroom with a skylight, soaking tub, and a double vanity.

The sixth floor boasts a “skylit” fitness and wellness room along with a roof terrace “awaiting the next owner’s finishing touch.”

Schlisser said every prospective buyer she has shown the home to is interested in living there full-time.

“Carnegie Hill is a wonderful neighborhood,” she said. “Culturally and educationally, everything is there and the most frequented museums are there as well as some of the best private schools in Manhattan.”

The detached carriage house has cathedral ceilings, vertical-grain Douglas fir paneling, and a sleeping loft that could be used for guest accommodations or additional recreation space.

“I think the next buyer will be someone who is looking for space and proximity to schools,” Schlisser added. “The style is all new but very much a pre-war style. Everything has been done with incredible care. It’s really beautiful.”

#5411. 2026 BCDA Grand: Foxgrove on Castleberry

Foxgrove on Castleberry redefines the build-to-rent (BTR) model as a complete neighborhood, blending the character of a single-family community with the flexibility of rental living. Located on a former farmstead between the North Georgia foothills and Lake Lanier, the 198-home development combines 161 townhomes and 37 detached homes, creating architectural diversity while accommodating residents at different life stages.

Rather than relying on a repetitive housing pattern, the community offers a mix of three- and four-bedroom homes ranging from approximately 1,700 to 2,300 square feet. Efficient floor plans provide generous living spaces, private outdoor areas, and the functionality expected of traditional homeownership. The combination of attached and detached residences allows the project to achieve density and operational efficiency while maintaining a human-scaled streetscape.

The site plan is shaped by the property’s natural features. Homes are organized around preserved green spaces, mature trees, pocket parks, and a restored freshwater pond, transforming the landscape into the community’s defining amenity. Nearly two miles of walking trails weave throughout the development, connecting residents to nature and encouraging daily interaction. A centrally located clubhouse, resort-style pool, fitness center, dog park, picnic areas, and outdoor gathering spaces further support an active and social neighborhood environment.

Award: GrandCategory: Build-to-RentDeveloper: Pine Grove CommunitiesArchitect: The KSE Group ArchitectureBuilder: KM HomesLocation: Atlanta

Foxgrove’s design emerged from significant site and entitlement challenges. Instead of treating these environmental features as obstacles, the design embraces them. Stream corridors were preserved, the existing pond was restored instead of replaced, and the community was carefully configured around the site’s natural systems.

By combining thoughtful land stewardship with a diversified housing mix, Foxgrove highlights how BTR communities can create lasting neighborhoods that are environmentally responsible, socially connected, and firmly rooted in their local context.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5410. 2026 BCDA Grand: Collection at R Street

In Washington, D.C.’s historic Shaw neighborhood, The Collection at R Street reveals how thoughtful infill development and adaptive reuse can expand housing opportunities while preserving neighborhood character. The 23-unit project embraces a “missing middle” housing strategy, bridging the gap between single-family homes and large multifamily developments through a mix of housing types within a single urban block.

At its center is the adaptive reuse of a 19th-century schoolhouse that had most recently served as offices. Rather than demolish the vacant structure, the team transformed it into 12 condominium residences, preserving key historic features while introducing modern living spaces. Original masonry, window openings, and roof forms were restored, while high ceilings, exposed roof trusses, and even historic blackboard walls were incorporated into the new design. Upgraded building systems and an enhanced envelope improve energy performance and ensure the building’s long-term viability.

The development also includes four new rowhouses on a former parking lot and a freestanding duplex on a triangular parcel. Both new-construction components draw inspiration from Shaw’s historic residential fabric through their scale, materiality, and relationship to the street.

By repurposing an existing landmark and converting underutilized land into housing, the project shows how preservation and sustainable development can work hand in hand. It delivers a diverse mix of homes in a transit-rich neighborhood while demonstrating how adaptive reuse, contextual design, and environmental stewardship can extend a building’s civic legacy for generations to come

#5409. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

“One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”

#5407. 2026 BCDA Grand: Sag Harbor Bay

When sustainability is at the core of a project’s design, rather than a collection of added-on features, its relationship with the landscape is symbiotic.

This home leverages indoor-outdoor connection refreshingly, with water views seen through the tree canopy, for an authentic experience.

Materials inside mirror those seen out the massive windows, such as mosaic stone, wide-plank, European heart oak floors, and warm cedar shingles that resemble tree bark. These all help to blur the boundaries between inside and out, making this home feel naturally rooted in the landscape.

#5405. President Woodrow Wilson’s Historic Princeton Home Lists for $5.85 Million After a 7-Year Restoration

The home where Woodrow Wilson lived as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” says listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

The estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell says the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

The three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with new matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell says.

Of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

“This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a new home,” Blackwell says. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

#5400. Housing Week Ahead: International Demand, Home Prices, and New-Home Sales

The coming week brings a number of key indicators and new research from the Realtor.com Economics team, despite the holiday schedule for Thanksgiving Day.

On Monday, new research from senior economist Hannah Jones shows that many Americans won't be traveling far to visit their parents for the holiday. That’s because a third of American adults under 35 years old still live in their parents’ home.

On Wednesday, senior economist Jiayi Xu has our third-quarter International Demand report, showing where home shoppers from different countries are looking at U.S. homes.

Also on Wednesday, coming out early due to the Thanksgiving holiday, senior economist Jake Krimmel will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest housing market trends in real time.

For economic indicators being released next week, we’ll see the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Index on Tuesday, along with new-home sales and the Freddie Mac mortgage rate on Wednesday.

The Case-Shiller Index is expected to show national home price growth holding near 2% through September, after the national index rose 2.1% year over year through August. Annual gains have climbed since the spring, but slower median sales price growth and softer contract activity this summer suggest the pickup may be running out of steam.

New-home sales are likely to show another weak month in October, after falling 5.3% year over year in September. The existing-home segment saw softer pending home sales and home purchase closings last month as buyers are faced with affordability challenges due to high mortgage rates.

Despite more builders offering mortgage rate buydowns, the new-home segment is expected to be slowed down as well, as buyers’ budgets are stretched thin.

One thing I’ll be watching closely is the median new-home sales price, which has been lower than the median existing-home sales price for much of 2026, an intriguing result that mostly stems from where the new homes being sold are located.

The Freddie Mac average mortgage rate, which will come out on Wednesday instead of its usual Thursday, is likely to remain in the low-7% range, as the 10-Year Treasury yield remains elevated above 5% in advance of the expected rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

#5399. Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

“We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller said. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”

#5398. A Legacy Built on Trust and Community

Long Companies, a member of Leading Real Estate Companies of the World®

Favorite part of your job: Helping agents find opportunities and ways to navigate through them

Motto or work philosophy that you live by: Be curious. We apply our own filters and biases when we think we know the answers, so when faced with a challenge, I get really curious about why things are happening, what people need, what has changed and how we can align around that.

What is the biggest challenge currently facing your brokerage?

Rather than looking at things as challenges, I view them as opportunities—and while I believe there’s an opportunity in everything that happens, it’s about navigating that. Right now we have a market that’s starting to soften a little bit and regulate, so the question is: what do people need, and how do we deliver that?

From an industry standpoint, it feels as though a lot of brokerages and brokerage models appear to be chasing one another, but I’m more focused on quality experiences. And that begins with quality agents and staff.

I also believe the human part of this is really important in real estate. We’ve seen time and again that people want to work with a human, so doubling down on that experience is critical as we deal with a changing market.

Long Realty has reached an incredible 100-year milestone. What has contributed to the company’s success and longevity?

Having survived World Wars, recessions, depressions and pandemics, the company is adaptable and resilient. Communication is key when it comes to educating our agents so they can take that information to the consumer. We don’t make decisions blindly, and people can get behind what we’re doing, as we’ve built up a level of trust over the years.

The other thing I would point to is that we’re community focused. In addition to our own foundation that gives millions of dollars to local nonprofits, we’re also engaged in community activities, causes and sponsorships.

We’ve spent a long time building out our brand. More than just a logo, it’s the way people feel about us. A big part of my job is being a steward of the brand, ensuring that we’re doing things that align with how we want to be known.

What leadership practices have been most important in building and sustaining Long Realty’s success?

For me, it’s about empowering the people I work with. Not only do you need to work together to establish your vision, but you also need to have buy-in and ensure that people are passionate about it. And that begins with having great people who fit the culture. I find that most people want to do a great job and feel fulfilled, so how do we help our staff and our agents do amazing things? It can’t be about one person. It’s a collective, and we’re here to help the collective be better.

How do the partnerships you enjoy as a LeadingRE network member impact your business?

While we have the HomeServices network and our sister companies that we work with, layering on an organization like LeadingRE expands our capabilities and footprint. Through LeadingRE, we’ve built a lot of relationships with brokers around the country and the world, which has allowed us to service more people. We’re also members of Luxury Portfolio, which is important given the fact that Long Realty has nearly 40% market share on the million-dollar-plus side in our community. The members match our culture, and we feel comfortable referring and working with these folks.

For more information, please visit https://www.leadingre.com.

#5396. Asking Mom and Dad for Down Payment Help This Thanksgiving? Here’s How Much To Ask For

Thanksgiving. A time for turkey, football, and the gathering of family.

It can be a stressful day for many, from the demands of traveling to the obligations of hosting at home. But hopefully, for most, it’s a day to be spent being thankful for having the loved ones gathered around the table.

And what better time to ask those loved ones for a bit of help to achieve the American dream than on a quintessential American holiday?

Jokes aside, if it’s on your holiday agenda to hit up Mom, Dad, Grandma, Grandpa, or even cool Aunt Janet for some money to buy a home next year, there’s a few things you should know before making the trip.

Like how much you’re actually going to need for that dream home.

The reality is, young people really do need help with down payments these days—and many are getting it.

In the past year, 25% of first-time homebuyers used gifts or loans from family and friends to help fund their down payment, according to the National Association of Realtors® 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers.

Furthermore, whether they’re going it alone or with help, all buyers are strapped for the cash for down payments as overall payments are on the decline.

The typical down payment share dropped for four straight quarters, softening to 12.8% in the first quarter of 2026, down 1.1 percentage points from a year earlier, according to the most recent Realtor.com® down payment report.

In dollar terms, down payments sank 19% year over year to their lowest point since the third quarter of 2021.

Before sitting down with your parents to talk numbers, it’s important to know just how much money you’ll actually need.

For context, the typical U.S. down payment in April 2026 reached $25,000, or an average of 13.2% of the purchase price, down from $27,500 and 13.8% in April 2025.

But calculating the right amount you’ll need starts with being honest about how much money you already have—and where you plan to buy.

"Every buyer’s situation and every market is different, so there’s no single number," Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones says. Still, there are benchmarks to keep in mind.

"The most useful targets are the 10% and 20% thresholds, and the right ask depends on how far a buyer is from the next one. In lower-cost metros, help reaching 10% down could be just a few thousand dollars rather than tens of thousands. In pricey California metros, the typical down payment is well into six figures, which is very hard to save without a windfall (see the AI boom) or parental help.”

Framing the request around those specific benchmarks should make it easier to explain to your parents why a certain dollar amount matters. Hitting each tier unlocks tangible savings on the loan itself, reducing ongoing housing costs long after closing day.

"Getting to 10% down can pay off significantly in the form of a lower mortgage rate, and getting to 20% eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance," Jones explains.

Still, asking for help is tricky, and if you’re concerned your parents will be hesitant, remember that any help they can offer will go a long way.

“A smaller loan still lowers the monthly payment. More is better if the goal is minimizing the payment, but reaching one of these thresholds is a great place to start the conversation."

Finally, if there is some hesitation from your family about offering a helping hand due to the market conditions and mortgage rates, there’s some hope on the horizon that should sway them.

"Nationally, the market has shifted in a more buyer-friendly direction," Jones says. But location truly makes all the difference.

"Supply is still catching up in many Northeast and Midwest metros, so sellers hold more of the cards there and buyers should put their best foot forward. In the South and parts of the West, buyers are in the driver’s seat.”

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. The XRP price is struggling to take advantage of institutional credibility for the ledger. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has another explanation: Wall Street is pulling liquidity toward blockbuster IPOs.

The XRP Ledger Foundation assessed the network against all ten principles in the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. CertiK independently verified the network’s evidence under the Architecture and Resiliency principles.

Garlinghouse said investors have been moving money out of crypto, including XRP, to fund major listings. He expects the market to recover after Anthropic’s debut, just as it did following SpaceX’s IPO.

This makes the assessment relevant to banks exploring tokenized markets. Institutions need to understand how networks handle operational risk, governance, and settlement before building financial products on them.

The XRP Ledger Foundation has completed the attestation of the XRP Ledger against the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit. It is the first public, permissionless layer-1 blockchain to have the toolkit's Architecture and Resiliency principles independently… pic.twitter.com/wEKczeEdrF

XRPL’s case is notable because it is public and permissionless. Traditional financial networks often operate behind controlled access. Public blockchains must show how risks are handled across distributed governance, protocol upgrades, and open participation.

The Foundation assessed XRPL against all ten principles. It also supplied supporting evidence for each control. CertiK then examined the Architecture and Resiliency sections, using code, configurations, logs, and test results.

CertiK said it reviewed all 112 controls in the toolkit. Its technical verification focused on those suitable for independent assessment. The firm also verified Partior’s self-attestation under the same two principles.

Institutional adoption of digital assets depends on trust backed by independent verification and evidence.CertiK has completed independent technical verification of @XRPLF’s and Partior’s self-attestations under the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit,… pic.twitter.com/nQoEXjDHLh

The XRPL Foundation called it the first such verification for a public, permissionless Layer 1. The milestone gives institutions a structured reference when evaluating networks for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, funds, and other assets.

That is useful progress for XRPL’s institutional pitch. Risk and compliance teams can now examine evidence against familiar market-infrastructure standards. They have more than a blockchain’s own description of its capabilities.

In the interview, Garlinghouse addressed the gap between Ripple’s expansion and XRP price performance. He said the SpaceX IPO triggered a similar pullback as investors shifted liquidity out of crypto. He specifically named Bitcoin and XRP among the assets affected.

Investors moved capital from liquid crypto markets into the highly anticipated SpaceX listing, he said. Garlinghouse sees the same pattern ahead of Anthropic’s debut.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The offering covers 980 million shares, and the deal is expected to close Friday, November 20.

“What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets,” Garlinghouse said. “I think you’ll see that happen here as well.”

He also expects digital assets to stop moving in lockstep. In his view, real utility and demand will increasingly separate stronger projects from speculative tokens. That puts the XRP price debate back on XRPL’s ability to attract activity.

#5394. Young Adults Living With Parents Surge Fastest in America’s Once-Affordable Regions

Young adults living with their parents have become a familiar symbol of America's housing affordability crisis. But the geography of that living arrangement is changing, according to new research.

A record 25.2 million Americans aged 18 to 34 lived with their parents in 2025, or roughly 1 in 3 young adults. Nationally, that share barely budged between the pooled 2020–22 and 2023–25 periods, according to The Geography of the Crowded Nest, a new report from Realtor.com®.

Beneath that apparent stability, however, the South and Midwest—long considered the nation's affordability havens—recorded the largest year-over-year increases in 2025, with the share living at home rising 1.4 percentage points to 32.3% and 31.7%, respectively.

Meanwhile, in the notoriously expensive Northeast—where living with parents has historically been most common—the rate fell 2.3 percentage points to 36.9%, its lowest level since 2010.

It pushes back against conventional logic that cheaper housing markets offer young adults an easier path to independence.

"This is not a coastal problem that has stayed coastal; it has spread to even the more-accessible parts of the country," writes Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com and author of the report.

Perhaps the clearest illustration comes from two metros that, at first glance, seem worlds apart: San Antonio, TX, and Boston, MA.

One is steeped in cowboy culture; the other, Ivy League academia. In October, the median asking rent in Boston was $2,954, more than double the $1,117 in San Antonio. Yet the share of young adults living with their parents was nearly identical: 33.6% in the Alamo City and 34.3% in Beantown.

“The short answer is that different affordability constraints can produce the same outcome,” says Jones.

Take the Midwest, where the median home listing price is nearly $183,000 below the Northeast's. It's a sizable gap that obscures the fact that prices in both regions have climbed at nearly the same pace since before the pandemic: 48.4% and 50.8%, respectively, according to data from Realtor.com.

Even excluding 18- to 24-year-olds, who may still be establishing their careers and are therefore more vulnerable to economic pressures, the Midwest reached a record: 14.8% of those ages 25 to 34 lived with their parents in 2025, the highest rate for that age group in 25 years.

At the same time, many affordable markets didn’t see the same run-up in local wages as they did in home prices, which only deepened the divide.

"In San Antonio, the problem is the wage-price gap," says Jones.

Geoffrey Sanzenbacher, an economist at Boston College who has studied the rise in young adults living with parents, points to another side of that relationship.

"The same things that might make an area expensive—lots of good jobs with good pay—also serve to keep people out of their parents' home," he tells Realtor.com.

"Areas with hot labor markets may see kids living with their parents because they can't afford an apartment. Areas with poor labor markets may see kids living with their parents because they can't find a job," he adds.

His September research found that higher rents were associated with greater co-residence among adults aged 25 to 34. Stronger employment and wages were associated with lower rates among men, although the relationship was not statistically significant among women.

Of the 20 major metros examined, 12 recorded increases between the pooled periods, while eight saw declines.

Las Vegas experienced the largest increase, followed closely by San Francisco and San Jose, CA—markets with vastly different housing costs. Even in Texas, San Antonio's rate climbed while Houston's fell.

One possible explanation lies in who benefits when housing becomes more available.

In San Antonio, active home listings are now more than 40% above pre-pandemic levels, according to Jones. Yet the metro recorded one of the largest increases in young adults living with their parents.

"By and large, the market has homes available, but local young adults can't qualify for them at current prices and rates," Jones says, noting that higher-earning newcomers and existing homeowners looking to trade up are better positioned to purchase those properties.

But San Antonio's rental market has also improved. Approximately 6,900 apartments were completed in 2025, according to Northmarq. By year's end, vacancies had reached 11.8% and asking rents had fallen 4.5%.

Boston offers a counterpoint. Jones suggests that new rental construction, combined with the metro's higher-paying industries, may have helped some young adults establish independent households despite a much tighter housing market.

"Markets where supply growth is concentrated in the mid-to-upper tiers still see entry-level households struggle to keep up," Jones says. "The lesson for other markets is about the type of supply that moves the co-residence needle."

There's one last side to the story of young adults moving back home: A growing number are opening their own homes to their parents.

In his research, Sanzenbacher found that the share of adults aged 25 to 34 hosting their parents increased from 1.6% in 1996 to 4% in 2025—a living arrangement outside the scope of the new co-residence figures from Realtor.com.

In Boston, George Sarkis, co-founder and CEO of The Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman, says some parents are helping adult children with down payments, while other families are considering shared living arrangements.

"It can also work in the other direction, with adult children helping aging parents while allowing everyone to remain close," he says.

Sarkis adds he's seeing buyers considering how a property can serve different generations over time. That can mean finding homes with private suites or separate living quarters that allow family members to maintain their independence.

"Living under the same roof doesn't necessarily mean sacrificing independence. With the right property and layout, it can be a strategic financial decision that benefits multiple generations," he adds.

But those arrangements can introduce another financial hurdle.

A separate analysis from Realtor.com found that homes marketed for multigenerational living in San Antonio received 65.2% more page views than standard listings in 2025. Yet their median asking price was $573,105—nearly 69% higher than standard homes.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5393. Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

Robotics component maker coprod Inc. announced today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

At the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the company’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

Coprod is tackling the issue wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”

The company claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The company is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the company’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the company’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

Component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

Delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, said coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.

#5392. Miley Cyrus Marries Maxx Morando in Tearful Palm Springs Ceremony—Inside Their Malibu Marital Mansion

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando exchanged vows in an intimate Palm Springs ceremony surrounded by their closest family and friends.

Cyrus, 33, wore a long-sleeved silk Saint Laurent gown with matching pumps. Morando, 28, wore a tuxedo jacket and trousers from the French fashion house.

A source said Cyrus was excited and a little nervous before the ceremony, and smiled through tears as she exchanged vows.

“It was such a beautiful ceremony. Miley was excited and a little nervous beforehand. During the vows, she kept smiling through her tears. She was trying to hold it together, but she was just so happy to be marrying Maxx," the insider told People.

The bride’s mother, Tish Cyrus, father, Billy Ray Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were among the guests. Billy Ray’s girlfriend, Elizabeth Hurley, and her son, Damian Hurley, also attended.

The couple wed poolside beneath an arch decorated with white flowers. The day before, they celebrated with loved ones at a rehearsal dinner, where the menu featured “M+M” at the top—a nod to their initials.

The news of their engagement was first confirmed in September 2025, after Cyrus was seen wearing a sparkling engagement ring as they posed together on the red carpet at the premiere of “Avatar: Fire and Ash.”

Cyrus and Morando have been linked since the summer of 2021. In a British Vogue cover interview, the “Flowers” singer recalled their introduction, explaining, “We got put on a blind date.”

She then provided a key clarifying detail, noting, “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’”

It’s safe to say the date was a success, with their love story blossoming over the last four years.

Almost immediately, they began collaborating together professionally, with Cyrus telling Vogue Morando was one of her “favorite emerging artists,” having designed sustainable looks for her to wear during her various appearances in music festivals in 2021.

Later that year, Morando’s band, Liily, performed as part of “Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party,” where the “Hannah Montana” star rang in the New Year with an NBC special.

He’s even collaborated on some of Cyrus’s most recent music, and in a Harper’s Bazaar interview, she explained the significance of bringing a romantic partner into her professional sphere.

“I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other,” she said. “I’ve always worked with the people that I love. And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

While Morando appears to be quite private in regards to his personal life, he has publicly supported his soon-to-be wife at a handful of public events, including movie premieres and award shows.

A few years into their relationship, the nearlyweds took a major leap. A People magazine source confirmed they had moved in together in February 2024.

“She is very happy with him,” the source revealed. “Miley has changed a lot in the past couple of years. She seems more calm and harmonious. Everyone loves Maxx. He’s a great guy. She is very happy with him. He’s private and doesn’t like being in the press. It’s been good for her.”

Cyrus shared what it’s like to live with her fiance in a September 2026 chat on the Zane Lowe Show, where she gushed that even life’s most mundane tasks are more fun with Morando around.

"I think that’s the thing that maybe generations prior didn’t teach us, that marriage doesn’t need to be a prison. It can actually be a playground,” she said. “It’s just living with a best friend. And that’s what it is.”

In 2024, an Us magazine source confirmed that although “Miley owns a number of properties,” the lovebirds are “staying at her home in Malibu,” which was described as a “huge mansion overlooking the water in a gated community.”

Although Cyrus also has homes in Studio City, Hidden Hills, and her home state of Tennessee, the couple reportedly adores the Malibu home’s proximity to the sea. Apparently, they “spend a lot of time on the private beach together.”

Cyrus has a long history of living in Malibu—and even has a song named after the coastal locale.

Back in 2016, she paid $2.5 million for a gorgeous midcentury modern home in the area. At the time, she shared the 1,385-square-foot dwelling with her now-ex-husband, Liam Hemsworth. The former couple used it as a creative studio and guest house.

The funky home was perched on a two-acre property with lots of lush greenery, which could be peacefully enjoyed from the terrace of the primary bedroom, according to Architectural Digest.

The singer and “The Hunger Games” star would call another Malibu mansion their home, however—a $6.8 million property Hemsworth had purchased in 2014, which was tragically destroyed by the 2018 Wolsey Fire just weeks before their wedding.

The sprawling property was more than just a home. It also housed Rainbowland, her personal recording studio.

Miley reflected on the tragedy in 2025, telling People, “When my house burned down, that was the biggest blessing I’ve ever had in my life, actually.”

She explained that after “losing everything,” having the opportunity “to rebuild” inspired her to be more “purposeful” when carefully selecting new belongings.

Cyrus and Hemsworth separated in August 2019, and their divorce was finalized in January 2020.

In the months following the split, Cyrus offloaded the guesthouse at a loss in an off-market transaction for $1.7 million, and Hemsworth sold the wildfire-damaged property for $3.6 million.

It wouldn’t be too long before the “Black Mirror” actress would find herself back in Malibu. She snapped up a $7.9 million Mediterranean mansion in the city in 2022, which is reportedly where she and Morando live now.

It’s truly a resort-like retreat, with a pool and spa in the backyard surrounded by soaring palm trees.

Indoors, an open-plan layout boasts tall ceilings and glass sliding doors that connect the serene space to the equally-tranquil landscape.

The massive primary suite provides striking panoramic views of the beach, and has a lounge space, a fireplace, and a balcony.

#5390. Many Sellers Feel Now Is the Time to Move, Despite High Rates: Report

Even with uncertainty keeping a hold on housing, many homeowners still feel now is the time to make their move in the market, according to a new report.

Century 21 Real Estate’s Home Seller Confidence Report found that 75% of homeowners planning to sell in the next 12 months believe now is the right time to move, and 82% who already have their homes on the market agree with the sentiment. The survey was conducted via Ipsos and included more than 1,000 current, prospective and recent home sellers across the country.

Despite the phenomena of the mortgage rate lock-in effect, Mike Miedler—president and CEO of Century 21 Real Estate—said that “people don’t make decisions about their homes based on rates alone,” and are often motivated by “new jobs, growing families and other life changes.”

“Sellers aren’t waiting for perfect conditions, but they are approaching that decision with more thought and preparation,” he continued. “They want to understand what their home is worth and how quickly it could sell so they can move forward with confidence.”

Taking a look at how mortgage rates affected seller decisions, rates ranked fifth among 16 factors in the report influencing the decision to move, coming in behind personal motivations such as finding the right next home, seeking a change of scenery and major life events.

The report also found that 86% of sellers surveyed said their mortgage rate was slightly, moderately, very or extremely influential on the timing of their move. Of sellers and homeowners with a mortgage under 5%. 54% did admit leaving behind their mortgage rate would be harder than leaving their home itself.

Even with motivation to move, the report outlined that homeowners do still have concerns slowing down their decisions. Specifically, more than 25% of sellers surveyed considered the choice of moving for one to two years or longer before listing their home.

Additionally, data showed that of sellers who sold in the last 2 years surveyed, 66% seriously reconsidered their asking price before listing at least once, with some revisiting the decision four or more times. Another 58% worried about pricing their home too high or ultimately having to reduce their asking price, while 27% worried about pricing too low.

“Today’s sellers are approaching one of life’s biggest financial decisions with more research and intention than ever before,” added Miedler. “They’re exploring pricing strategies, evaluating buyer demand and looking for trusted guidance before bringing their homes to market. The sellers who feel most confident are often the ones who have a clear strategy from the start.”

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5389. Inside Jensen Huang’s $53 Million Property Portfolio as the Nvidia CEO Is Reinstated After Affair With Suspected Chinese Spy

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia's CEO, less than three weeks after stepping down over two extramarital affairs. The relationships involved Alice Huang—a business executive whom the U.S. government has determined is working with Chinese intelligence—and a Nvidia employee.

The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO, and a board director, effective immediately, Nvidia announced on Nov. 23.

Interim CEO Colette Kress will return to her role as chief financial officer, and Harvey Jones will remain board chair.

In a statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his return serves the interests of its shareholders, employees, partners, and customers.

Huang said he was grateful for the board’s confidence and for the support of his family, Nvidia employees, shareholders, and industry partners.

As Huang returns to Nvidia, Realtor.com® has lifted the lid on the tech titan's expansive property portfolio.

Before transforming his company to the first in the world to reach a valuation of $5 trillion after seeing unprecedented growth amid the artificial intelligence boom, Huang spent his early childhood in Thailand.

He moved to the U.S. after his father visited America and vowed to bring his sons, he previously told CNBC.

Ahead of his move, his mom would teach him 10 words from the dictionary each day to help him learn English, despite not knowing the language herself.

At age 9, Huang and his brother headed to the U.S. to live with their relatives. His early life in the States was starkly different from the current lavish life he lives.

When he was a child, his aunt and uncle accidentally enrolled him in a Baptist boarding school in Kentucky, thinking it was a prestigious prep school. While there, he became a target for bullies and teasing due to his long hair and accent.

He has also followed in the footsteps of his fellow tech titans by pouring a sizable chunk of his fortune into real estate—amassing an incredibly impressive portfolio of homes from Hawaii to California.

In 2017, Huang splashed out more than $38 million for a sprawling mansion in San Francisco's Gold Coast neighborhood.

Property records seen by Realtor.com reveal that the dwelling is linked to Riva LLC, which is managed by Michael A. Chojnacki, a tax lawyer who looks after the finances of Huang and his wife, Lori.

The luxe abode in the Pacific Heights neighborhood spans 11,400 square feet and boasts a curved roof, panoramic views of the Golden Gate Bridge, and many bedrooms and bathrooms.

The limestone mansion has a large terrace, a three-car garage, two wine rooms, an outdoor kitchen, an elevator, a theater, and a gym.

Developer Bill Campbell of Marble Management previously told The Wall Street Journal that construction on the dwelling took nearly four years.

Huang is also neighbors with Larry Ellison and David Sachs.

Huang previously owned two starter homes in San Jose, CA. The first one, which measured 1,500 square feet and had three bedrooms, was sold for $185,000 in 1988—just five years before he founded Nvidia.

Elsewhere in California, the tech titan owns a lavish dwelling in Los Altos, just 15 miles west of Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara County.

He purchased the property in 2003 for $6.9 million. It measures over 7,000 square feet and has six bedrooms.

The elegant two-story estate features lush landscaping and a resort-style pool.

To top off his property portfolio, the businessman also snapped up a home on the south side of Maui in 2004.

The dwelling is situated in the Wailea Resort, which houses 14 other properties behind a gate and spans 10.5 acres on the ocean.

The home features seven bedrooms and was built in 2008. He paid $7.8 million for the abode.

The property spans 8,000 square feet and is surrounded by lush greenery.

In 2023, Maui experienced deadly wildfires, and the Huangs "donated significantly to local relief efforts,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

According to The New York Times, Nvidia is responsible for making "the most essential and expensive component in almost every A.I. scheme," a collection of hardware designed specifically to bolster artificial intelligence.

Its ascent to the pinnacle of tech success began as something of a slow burn in 1993, when Huang, 63, launched the company alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.

At the time, Nvidia was viewed very much as a niche—and fledgling—tech startup. However, it has since grown into an industry giant, inking deals with all manner of brands and agencies, from the U.S. Department of Energy to Nokia, Samsung, and Sam Altman's company, OpenAI, the parent of ChatGPT.

Huang's own net worth has skyrocketed with that accelerated growth. He is currently one of the 10 richest men in the world with an estimated fortune of $174 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The number of men who can claim to top him in personal fortune can be counted on two hands—and include the likes of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Ellison.

Like others in the exclusive "super billionaires" club—men and women with net worths exceeding $50 billion—Huang has invested his fortune across diverse ventures and companies, while managing to remain in this elite group.

#5388. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.
